steps.user_message: I want to file my 2023 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Chicago IL. W-2 from Metro Consulting: $82,350. Additional income: $11,200 (marketing, 2 clients), $1,780 from Marcus savings account, $320 from TD Ameritrade. Home office: 140 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,100/month for 780 sq ft. Deductions: $4,800 student loan interest (FedLoan, 2018–2019); $1,400 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt; $650 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — useful detail. Below is a practical, accurate breakdown for 2023 based on what you gave, plus next steps and the forms you’ll need.

Main points / what to report
- W-2 wages: Metro Consulting — $82,350 → report on Form 1040 (W-2 information).
- Self-employment / contract income: $11,200 → report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). Even if you didn’t get 1099s, you must report it.
- Interest income: $1,780 (Marcus) + $320 (TD Ameritrade) = $2,100 → report on Form 1040. Because total interest > $1,500, you’ll need Schedule B.
- Student loan interest: you paid $4,800 (2018–2019 FedLoan). The student loan interest deduction is an above-the-line deduction (adjusts your AGI) but the maximum allowed is $2,500 for 2023. There are income phase‑outs that may reduce/eliminate the deduction for higher incomes — see “phase-out check” below.
- Charitable: $1,400 cash gift with receipt → deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). If you take the standard deduction, you cannot also deduct this.
- Unreimbursed expenses ($650): These are not deductible for employees (W-2) for 2018–2025 (suspended by TCJA). If these are business expenses related to the $11,200 self‑employment income, include them on Schedule C instead.

Home office
- You report a home office deduction only if you are self‑employed (Schedule C). W‑2 employees generally cannot claim it.
- You have exclusive-use home office of 140 sq ft in a 780 sq ft home.
  - Simplified method: $5/sq ft × 140 sq ft = $700 (max 300 sq ft). No Form 8829 required.
  - Actual-expense method (example using rent only): annual rent = $2,100 × 12 = $25,200. Office share = 140 / 780 ≈ 17.95%. Rent portion = $25,200 × 17.95% ≈ $4,523. You can also allocate utilities, renters insurance, etc., to increase the deduction.
- Important: home office deduction cannot exceed your net profit from the business. If allocated home office + other business expenses exceed your self‑employment profit, the excess may be limited and some disallowed expenses can carry forward (Form 8829 handles this).

Self-employment tax
- Net profit from Schedule C is subject to self‑employment tax (Schedule SE) — roughly 15.3% on net earnings (more precisely, SE tax = 15.3% × 92.35% of net earnings). You can deduct half of your self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.

Itemize vs. standard deduction (quick guidance)
- 2023 standard deduction for Married Filing Jointly = $27,700.
- Your reported potential itemizable amount (so far) is only $1,400 charitable + whatever state & local taxes (SALT) or mortgage interest you paid (you didn’t list those). Without other sizable deductions, itemizing will likely be far less than $27,700.
- Recommendation (based on your numbers): Most likely take the standard deduction and claim the $2,500 student loan interest above-the-line (if eligible). Charitable deduction would only help if you have other itemizable deductions to bring total above $27,700.

Student loan interest phase-out (check)
- The student loan interest deduction has an income phase-out. Based on the incomes you gave (W‑2 $82,350 + self‑employment $11,200 + interest ~$2,100 = ~ $95,650 pre-adjustments), you are likely below the MFJ phase-out range and would be able to claim the full $2,500 maximum. Still, you should confirm using your actual modified AGI (after adjustments) because phase-out thresholds depend on MAGI.

Forms you will likely need (federal)
- Form 1040 (main return)
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments to Income) — student loan interest deduction and half of SE tax (as an adjustment)
- Schedule B — if interest and dividend total > $1,500 (you have $2,100 interest)
- Schedule C — report your $11,200 marketing/self‑employment income and business expenses (including home office if self‑employed)
- Schedule SE — calculate self‑employment tax
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (only if you use the actual-expense method for the home office). If you use the simplified $5/sq ft method, you do not file Form 8829.
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (for charitable contributions, SALT up to $10k cap, mortgage interest, etc.)
- Forms 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC, 1099-INT, 1099-B — as supporting documents for income (you should attach or keep them for records; the amounts still go on the schedules listed).

State filing
- Illinois resident: file IL-1040 and report federal AGI as a starting point. Illinois has no special city income tax on top of state in the return; check withholding on W-2 and estimated payments.

Documentation to keep
- W-2 and any 1099s (1099-NEC if clients issued one, 1099-INT for bank/broker interest, 1099-B if brokerage generated one)
- Records/receipts for charitable contributions (you have a receipt for $1,400)
- Student loan interest statement (Form 1098-E) or loan account statement
- Records supporting home office (measurements, lease/rent statements, utility bills, calculations)
- Receipts/invoices for any business expenses

Example (illustrative) quick math for home office choice
- Simplified home office deduction: $700.
- Actual rent allocation (rent only): ~$4,523. If you have enough net business profit and utilities to support it, actual method likely gives a larger deduction — but it’s limited by net profit. If your net self-employment income before home office is low, simplified might be more practical.

What I recommend you do next
1. Confirm whether the $11,200 is all self‑employment (i.e., reportable on Schedule C) and whether the $650 unreimbursed expenses relate to that business (if yes, include them on Schedule C).
2. Confirm you have Form 1098‑E (or year‑end loan statement) showing student loan interest paid.
3. Decide whether you want to use the simplified or actual home‑office method — I can run the numbers both ways if you give me any other home‑related expenses (utilities, renters insurance) and any other business expenses.
4. If you’d like, I can prepare an estimate of:
   - taxable income,
   - estimated self‑employment tax,
   - and whether the standard deduction is better for you (I can compute both scenarios).

If you want me to compute the numbers now, tell me:
- Is the $650 business-related (or W‑2 employee unreimbursed)?
- Any other business expenses or deductions not listed?
- Any state/local taxes paid (property tax, state income tax withheld) or mortgage interest (if applicable)?
- Whether you want me to use simplified or actual home office method (or I can show both).

If you prefer, I can also list the step‑by‑step items to hand your tax preparer.
